title: What HTML Is, How It Structures Documents and What It Does Not Do
learningObjectives: Define HTML as a standardized markup language used to describe the structure and meaning of web documents.
Distinguish an HTML tag, element, attribute, text node and comment using a concrete source example.
Explain the roles of start tags, end tags, nested elements and void elements, and recognize why valid nesting matters.
Distinguish HTML source text from the DOM tree constructed by the browser parser.
Explain how semantic elements communicate purpose and document structure to browsers, search systems and assistive technologies.
Compare semantic elements such as main, nav, article and button with generic containers such as div and span.
Explain why HTML does not replace CSS for presentation or JavaScript for general-purpose program logic.
Identify the relationship between HTML attributes, element properties and browser-provided behaviour at a conceptual level.
Explain how document language, headings, landmarks, links, forms and native controls contribute to accessibility and usability.
Recognize that browsers may recover from malformed markup, and explain why successful display does not prove that source markup is valid or well structured.
Use the HTML specification and browser Developer Tools as references when investigating element behaviour.
Choose meaningful HTML elements for a simple interface and justify the choice based on content semantics rather than default appearance.

understand.concept: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standardized markup language used to describe the structure and meaning of web documents. It marks content as headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, forms, navigation and other kinds of elements. A browser parses HTML source and constructs a live Document Object Model (DOM), which other browser technologies can inspect and modify. HTML is not a general-purpose programming language: it does not by itself provide the normal variables, loops, functions and decision-making used to express arbitrary algorithms. CSS describes presentation; JavaScript supplies programmable behaviour.
understand.whyItMatters: HTML is the foundation on which styling, scripting, accessibility and many browser features depend. Choosing the correct element gives content meaning and often provides useful behaviour automatically. A native button is keyboard-operable by default; a heading contributes to document structure; a link represents navigation. Replacing these with generic elements and recreating behaviour manually makes a page harder to use and maintain.
understand.history: HTML emerged with the early World Wide Web as a way to structure linked documents. It has evolved through multiple versions and standards processes. Modern HTML is maintained as a living standard, with elements and APIs defined for interoperable browser behaviour. Avoid treating old presentational markup or obsolete elements as modern best practice.
understand.analogy: HTML is like the outline and labelled sections of a technical document. It tells readers and software what each part represents, while a separate presentation layer controls how the document looks.
understand.analogyLimit: HTML is not merely a visual outline and does not prescribe one fixed appearance. Browsers apply default styles, but the meaning of an element is distinct from its default visual rendering. The DOM is also a parsed runtime structure, not simply a copy of the original source text.

explain.narrative:
A browser receives HTML as text and parses it according to HTML parsing rules. Consider `

Product guide

`. The characters `

` form a start tag, `Product guide` is text content, and `

` is an end tag. Together they form an h1 element. An attribute adds information to an element, as in `Help`: href supplies the link destination. Some elements are void elements and do not have end tags; for example, img and input. Their attributes provide the information they need. Elements can contain other elements, creating a nested document structure. Correct nesting matters because the browser's parser follows defined error-recovery rules. A page may still appear even when the source contains mistakes, so visual appearance alone is not a conformance check. Use a validator and inspect the constructed DOM when necessary. Choose elements by meaning. Use headings for headings, p for paragraphs, nav for a navigation region, main for the page's primary content, article for self-contained content, button for an action and a for navigation to a resource. A div is a generic block container and span is a generic phrasing container; use them when no more meaningful element fits. Do not choose an element only because its default appearance looks convenient. HTML source and the DOM are related but different. The browser parses the source, may normalize or repair malformed markup, and creates a live node tree. JavaScript can later change that tree without rewriting the original source file. Developer Tools' Elements panel shows the live DOM; View Source shows the delivered source text. HTML does not control every aspect of a web page. CSS rules determine presentation and layout. JavaScript can respond to events, update the DOM and communicate with APIs. HTML remains essential because it provides the document structure and native semantics those technologies build upon. Use valid, semantic HTML first; then add CSS and JavaScript to meet the design and behaviour requirements.

examples.code:
My first page

This page has meaningful content.
examples.explanation: The h1 element represents the main heading, while the p element represents a paragraph. HTML gives content structure and meaning; CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds programmable behaviour.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser displays the meaningful HTML content.

examples.title: Read the parts of an HTML element
examples.code: HTML guide start tag href attribute name "/guides/html" attribute value HTML guide text content end tag
examples.explanation: The start and end tags delimit an element. Attributes provide additional information. The element includes its tags, attributes and content. Attribute values must be quoted when required by HTML syntax and are best consistently quoted.
examples.expectedOutput: You can identify a tag, element, attribute and text content separately.

examples.title: Nested elements and void elements
examples.code:
Account settings

Update your contact details.
examples.explanation: The strong element is nested inside the paragraph. The img element is a void element: it has no closing tag and uses attributes such as src and alt. Correct nesting helps preserve the intended document structure.
examples.expectedOutput: A main region containing a heading, paragraph and image.

examples.title: Choose elements by purpose
examples.code:
Developer Journal

Articles About

Learning HTML

Semantic structure helps people and software understand content.
examples.explanation: The elements describe the purpose of each region. Semantic elements can improve navigation for assistive technology and make source code easier for developers to understand. Their default styling is not the reason to choose them.
examples.expectedOutput: A document with header, navigation, main content and an article.

examples.title: Source HTML and the live DOM are not identical views
examples.explanation: The original HTML source contains the text Waiting. After the script runs, the live DOM contains Ready. View Source and the Elements panel therefore answer different questions.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser displays Ready while the original source still contains Waiting.

examples.title: Separate structure, presentation and behaviour
examples.code:
<button class="primary-action" type="button" id="save">Save changes</button>

/* CSS */
.primary-action { padding: .75rem 1rem; }

// JavaScript
const saveButton = document.querySelector("#save");
saveButton.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("Save action requested");
});
examples.explanation: HTML provides a native action control, CSS styles it and JavaScript responds to the click. A real save operation would also need validation, error handling and a trusted persistence mechanism.
examples.expectedOutput: A semantic button with styling and a click response.

practise.guidedTask: Inspect the example and label every element, attribute and text node. Replace one generic div with a suitable semantic element and explain why it is more meaningful. Add a link, a button and an image with appropriate attributes. Open the page in a browser and compare View Source with the live DOM after a small JavaScript change.
practise.independentTask: Create a semantic article page containing a header, navigation, main region, article, section, heading hierarchy, paragraph, link, list, image with appropriate alternative text and a native button. Explain why each element was selected. Add one CSS rule and one JavaScript event listener without mixing their responsibilities into the HTML markup.
hints: An element is more than a tag name: it includes its attributes and content.
Use an end tag for normal elements that have one; void elements such as img and input do not have closing tags.
Choose elements based on meaning and behaviour, not their default visual appearance.
Use a for navigation to another resource and button for an action performed on the current interface.
Use div and span only when a more meaningful element is not appropriate.
The Elements panel shows the live DOM; View Source shows the delivered HTML source.
Browsers may recover from invalid markup. Use a validator rather than relying only on what appears on screen.
HTML semantics support accessibility but do not replace testing with assistive technologies.

questions.prompt: What is HTML primarily responsible for?
questions.explanation: HTML describes document structure and meaning.

questions.prompt: How does a browser use HTML?
options: Parses document structure and builds a DOM
Always treats it only as an image
questions.answer: Parses document structure and builds a DOM
questions.explanation: The DOM represents document nodes and their relationships.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines an HTML element?
options: The element's tags, attributes and content as a structural unit
questions.answer: The element's tags, attributes and content as a structural unit
questions.explanation: An element is the complete structural unit represented by its tags, attributes and content where applicable.

questions.prompt: Which element is normally the best choice for an action that submits or changes something on the current page?
questions.explanation: A native button represents an action and provides built-in interactive semantics and keyboard behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why can View Source and the Elements panel show different text?
options: The Elements panel shows the live DOM, which scripts may have changed after parsing.
View Source always displays CSS only.
questions.answer: The Elements panel shows the live DOM, which scripts may have changed after parsing.
questions.explanation: The browser constructs a DOM from source and scripts can modify that live tree without rewriting the original response.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason to use semantic HTML elements?
options: They always have more attractive default colours.
They communicate the purpose and structure of content to browsers, users and assistive technology.
They remove the need for CSS.
questions.answer: They communicate the purpose and structure of content to browsers, users and assistive technology.
questions.explanation: Semantic elements describe meaning and can provide native behaviour and accessibility benefits.
